stories.body:
A graphic novel by Melissa Chan and Badiucao imagines China and the US at war in 2035. They hope to remind young people that ‘authoritarianism everywhere is bad’

D rinking Tsingtao beers, eating congee, walking with hands behind their backs: for many young people in western countries, “ Chinamaxxing ” has become all the rage. Some content creators have even gone beyond the jokes about being in “a very Chinese time in my life” and have followed this passion to the Middle Kingdom: making TikToks in Chongqing’s multi-layered metropolis, bathing in Chengdu’s 24-hour spas, or backflipping on the Great Wall of China.

This irreverent, mostly ironic trend is jarring for some, but Chinese-Australian artist Badiucao and Chinese-American journalist Melissa Chan don’t want to lecture the so-called Chinamaxxers.

“The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society. They feel defeated when they see what’s happening in Gaza – there’s been protests but the government doesn’t care and is collaborating with atrocities in wars. There’s also the Epstein files in America, which show how the elite is corrupt,” says Badiucao, who, along with Chan, is in Sydney to promote their new book, You Must Take Part in Revolution.

“When you want to see change, there is the hard way, which is being innovative and finding a solution. And there is the lazy way, which is finding a cheap alternative and fantasising about a faraway, oriental, communist country that might be your future,” he says.

Chan and Badiucao have both paid the price for criticising China’s one-party system. Chinese officials refused to renew Chan’s press credentials before expelling the former Al Jazeera journalist from China in 2012; and the previously anonymous political cartoonist Badiucao was forced to reveal his identity in 2019 after it was compromised and authorities threatened his family in China.

You Must Take Part in Revolution, the pair’s debut graphic novel, portrays a dystopian future where China is at war with the United States in 2035.

The graphic novel features a variety of characters from the Chinese-speaking diaspora, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, the US and Tibet, as they decide what choices they are willing to make under authoritarian oppression.

“It was intentional to show the panoply of Asian identities that have been impacted by a great power,” Chan says. “It opens up the possibility to get young people to better understand it’s not just a ‘Chinese time in my life’, that there’s a lot going on here … hopefully it can get a few people thinking about resistance movements both present and in the past.”

“We don’t want to just lecture,” Badiucao adds. “We really want readers to put themselves in the eyes of those characters as if they were a real human being with a real life.”

Chan now lives in Berlin and has written for the Atlantic, the Washington Post, Time, and others, while Badiucao, who lives in Melbourne, has exhibited works across the world. They started working on the graphic novel five years ago after first meeting in Germany during the late 2010s.

You Must Take Part in Revolution starts off in the real-life Hong Kong protests of 2019, when almost two million people took to the streets to denounce a controversial law that would allow the extradition of suspects to mainland China. The law was viewed as a sign of growing mainland influence in Hong Kong.

While the graphic novel is geographically grounded in an Asia governed by authoritarian China, it also portrays the US as a proto-fascist state, resisting the idea that criticising one necessarily means painting the other in a positive light.

“This book happens to focus on China, but authoritarianism everywhere is bad,” Chan says. “We don’t want anyone to engage in whataboutism and I don’t think there needs to be a balance – if things are shit, they’re shit in any country.”

Unlike other graphic novels such as Art Spiegelman’s Maus, Badiucao and Chan’s book takes its influence from Japanese manga. “There are great works like Attack on Titan which are not necessarily about specific history or political content that have so many metaphors reflecting important things like racism, war and equity,” Badiucao says.

“It’s part of the reason this form is potentially more than just entertainment or some kid stuff, it really influences an entire generation.”

You Must Take Part in Revolution was released in the US and UK in 2025, but it is only just getting its Australian release this week.

Badiucao says readers across the world have contacted them about their own histories after reading it, including Ukrainian refugees who have escaped Russia’s invasion, and Czech communities who lived through the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.

The artist recalls one interaction at a comic festival in New York, where a second-generation Chinese Canadian girl told him that she had hesitations about taking the book home. “I don’t think my mum would love it,” she said.

A few minutes later, an older woman came up to Badiucao and explained she was an immigrant whose family had been through hardship during the Cultural Revolution. Flipping through the book, she said her daughter might like it, but she didn’t know if she would be open to learning about Chinese politics.

Badiucao later discovered the two were mother and daughter.

“I told the daughter her mum might be more open about political stuff, and I told the mum that your daughter might be interested too,” he says. “They ended up having an honest conversation, and they got a copy of the book … among all the interactions with readers, that was pretty special to me.”

You Must Take Part in Revolution by Melissa Chan and Badiucao is out now in Australia (Affirm Press; $39.99), as well as in the US and UK.

stories.title: Trump tells FCC to punish journalist for calling his election results "mixed"
stories.summary: Trump furious at NBC's Kristen Welker for saying he had mixed results in primary endorsements.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Trump furious at NBC’s Kristen Welker for saying he had mixed results in primary endorsements.

President Trump yesterday demanded that the Federal Communications Commission punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in his election endorsements. In the latest example of how Trump is using the FCC to harass reporters and news organizations that he dislikes, he said Meet the Press host Kristen Welker “will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment” for what he claimed was a “purposeful inaccuracy.”

“Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates, when the recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm. How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post .

A separate post from Trump yesterday said, “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT.” Trump also posted a rant on Friday about New York Times journalist Maggie Haberman, calling her “an unattractive person both inside and out” who “should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me.” Trump referred to Haberman throughout his post as “Maggot Haberman.”

Trump’s post about Welker included an image purporting to show he has near-perfect results in his endorsements this year. “The Press is a Disgrace to our Nation, and I hope that Chairman Brendan Carr, and the fine people of his Commission, will take this Threat to our Country very seriously,” Trump wrote.

Perhaps indicating that he will refer additional journalists for FCC punishment, Trump wrote that Welker “is not the only one. The Radical Left News is going out of their way to harass, demean, and libel anything ‘TRUMP.’”

Trump’s FCC chair has eagerly obeyed orders

The idea of the FCC punishing reporters for basic analysis of election results would have seemed far-fetched in previous administrations. The FCC website says the commission “cannot prevent the broadcast of any particular point of view,” and that it “generally will not intervene” in complaints about “one-sided news reports” because “it would be inconsistent with the First Amendment to replace the journalistic judgment of licensees with our own.”

Even during Trump’s first term, then-FCC Chairman Ajit Pai said that under the First Amendment, “the FCC does not have the authority to revoke a license of a broadcast station based on the content of a particular newscast.” Pai made the comment less than a week after Trump called on the FCC to revoke broadcast licenses from NBC and other networks for “fake news.”

An FCC investigation of Welker over an ordinary statement about election results seems much less far-fetched under Carr, who has embraced his role as Trump’s chief censor. Carr has made it clear he takes orders from Trump , abandoning his previous position—which he held under Democratic presidents —that the FCC must operate independently of White House interference.

Welker said in an appearance on NBC 4 Washington that Trump “has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries” and that “he’s had some mixed results but most recently his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course the sister of the late Senator Lindsay Graham, was successful in her primary battle.” Trump’s post attacking Welker claimed that “the story of [Graham’s] Victory was hardly covered by anybody,” despite Welker mentioning it in the very statement that triggered Trump’s wrath.

Poynter Senior Media Writer Tom Jones writes , “What Welker said about Trump’s endorsements having mixed results was true. Trump just didn’t like it.” While Trump praised himself for his successful endorsements, he didn’t mention primary losses by Republican gubernatorial candidates Burt Jones in Georgia and Randy Feenstra in Iowa and the failed re-election bid by Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida).

Carr uses news-distortion policy to threaten networks

An NBC News spokesperson told several media outlets that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her.” We contacted NBC News and will update this article if it has any further comment.

Welker is hardly the first TV journalist to discuss Trump’s mixed endorsement results. “Already, just this month alone, six of the president’s endorsed candidates have lost their races, and so there are questions about the power of his endorsements,” CNN White House correspondent Alayna Treene said on Inside Politics .

In June, Trump abruptly ended an interview with Welker after she challenged his claims of election rigging in California. Trump stated that “all I have to do is look” when Welker asked him for evidence of cheating. “That’s not evidence,” Welker responded.

If Carr does investigate Welker, he could do so under the FCC’s news distortion policy. Carr has repeatedly invoked the rarely enforced news distortion policy and a rule against broadcast hoaxes in various threats to Trump’s perceived enemies in the media. We asked the FCC chairman’s office today if the commission will investigate Welker and will update this article if we get a response.

Previous FCC leaders set such a high bar for proving news distortion that the policy was all but abandoned until Carr made it a focal point of his attempts to punish broadcasters. In September 2025, Carr threatened to revoke ABC station licenses for news distortion if they continued airing Jimmy Kimmel’s show.

Trump and FCC try to reshape the media

While Carr can cause trouble for licensed broadcasters and networks simply by issuing threats, he went far beyond mere threats in the case of ABC. The Carr FCC ordered ABC to file early license-renewal applications for the eight TV stations it owns and operates and justified the proceeding by accusing ABC of violating anti-discrimination rules with diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) practices.

ABC owner Disney is fighting back with a lawsuit against Carr and the FCC , saying it has faced a campaign of censorship in retaliation for the protected speech of its journalists and network programs. Both conservative and liberal groups have urged the FCC to back off.

The Trump administration has also sought to reshape the media through merger approvals. Paramount won FCC approval to buy Skydance after agreeing to install what Carr called a “bias monitor” at CBS. Paramount later won Justice Department approval to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, months after CEO David Ellison reportedly told Trump administration officials that he would make big changes at the Warner-owned CNN.

In March, Trump and Carr demanded more positive media coverage of the Iran war, with Carr claiming without evidence that broadcasters aired “hoaxes and news distortions.” Last year, Carr accused Comcast of news distortion when its subsidiary NBC refused to adopt the Trump administration narrative on the deportation of Kilmar Abrego Garcia.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the commission’s only Democrat, responded to Trump’s latest threat yesterday. “As I’ve said many times, the FCC has no authority to punish journalists this administration doesn’t like,” Gomez wrote . “These threats to press freedom are dangerous. They undermine the foundation of our democracy, and they have no place in it.”

stories.title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Andrew Bailey warns G20
stories.summary: The governor of the Bank of England warned of AI's “volatility” caused by energy shocks from the US-Iran war.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 hours ago

The governor of the Bank of England has warned G20 finance ministers that artificial intelligence could cause a global economic downturn and pose a significant cyber security risk to financial systems.

Andrew Bailey said any collapse of growth in the AI sector could lead to a "future market correction" that spreads worldwide.

In an open letter to finance ministers in the US on Monday, he said companies around the world should prepare for security breaches "involving simultaneous disruption across multiple firms".

Earlier this month, a group of 100 firms , including Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI, urged countries and groups to beef up their cyber defences before AI grows powerful enough to override them.

Bailey told the G20 finance ministers that a combination of highly priced stock markets, increased borrowing by investors, and the growing concentration of money into a small number of major technology companies could amplify any future market correction.

"The issue is not simply that investors are borrowing more, but that leverage is interacting with high valuations and market concentration, in particular the increasing cross-investment between artificial intelligence (AI) companies and hyper scalers, in a way that could amplify a future market correction," he said.

Bailey has called on those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis".

Bailey, who was writing in his capacity as chairman of the Financial Stability Board international watchdog (FSB), expressed concern about the "volatility" prompted by the effect of energy supply shocks caused by the US-Iran war.

His warning comes several months after UK Chancellor John Healey announced a £100m fund aimed at backing British AI start-ups .

That is part of the government's efforts to grow the country's "sovereign AI" capacity, developing homegrown AI technology to ensure the UK is not dependent on services from abroad.

Ministers want to see companies compete for the funding to help tackle challenges like cutting waiting lists in the NHS and bolstering cybersecurity and defence.

A UK government spokesperson said its' new AI economics institute was working with international partners to build "a stronger shared understanding of how AI is transforming economies around the world."

"The institute is the first government-backed body of its kind focused on AI's economic impact, helping policymakers understand what AI means for growth, productivity, jobs and public services as the technology develops at pace," the spokesperson said.

But there is growing concern that AI companies are increasingly developing models that can easily override the safeguarding systems of banks and financial centres.

Andrew Bailey wants those in charge of financial security to develop "appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release"

This summer has seen OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta all reveal their AI tools doing things they should not, with some AI agents going so far as to impersonate real people in order to get past security hurdles.

The FSB which Bailey leads is a global watchdog which monitors finance ministry officials, banks and securities regulators. It includes officials from the US, UK, France, Germany, Canada, Japan, Australia, China and Saudi Arabia.

stories.body:
Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods

Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12 hydropower projects in Nepal after the devastating flash floods , ​the ⁠country’s disaster ​management authority has said.

The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border.

About 500 of the missing hydropower workers at projects damaged by the flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts are thought to be trapped in tunnels built to control the flow of water.

As rescue efforts drag on, experts fear the chances of finding survivors in tunnels are diminishing as oxygen levels fall.

Some workers called for help when flooding started on Wednesday and those who had managed to escape tunnels said many of their colleagues were still trapped, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, the president of the Nepal Independent Power Producers’ Association.

Rescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access.

The swollen Trishuli River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.

Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testing on the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region.

Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters.

About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing.

The damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels.

Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.”

His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them.

The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.”

Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe.

“Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.”

The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.”

The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions .

Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage.

“Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said.

Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain.

“There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.”

Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis.

Among those missing are more than 30 British nationals. On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to support Britons and their families. The UK government has given a £5m support package to assist Nepal in its disaster response.

Amid the soaring toll of death and missing was some hope. On Monday, rescuers pulled a six-year-old girl out of mud after hearing crying. “Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside,” the Nepali armed police spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Agence France-Presse.

China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least ​220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing.

Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues.

Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers.

The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts.

In the holy ​town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells of what had once been ​homes , trying to salvage their belongings from the debris.

The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying ​it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau.

Two ​Nepali officials said China had ​not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness.

China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests.

stories.title: Mel Stride and Priti Patel replaced in major Tory reshuffle
stories.summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is shaking up her top team ahead of the party's conference in October.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 31 August 2026, 13:15 BST

Sir Mel Stride and Dame Priti Patel have left the shadow cabinet as part of a significant reshuffle of the Conservative top team by leader Kemi Badenoch.

Andrew Griffith will replace Sir Mel as shadow chancellor, while Tom Tugendhat will take the place of Dame Priti as shadow foreign secretary.

Badenoch is forming a new shadow cabinet before the party's conference in October.

With most polls putting the Conservatives in third place, lagging behind Labour and Reform UK, the Tory leader will be hoping a refreshed shadow cabinet will help boost her party's popularity.

Claire Coutinho, previously the shadow energy secretary, after her maternity leave will replace Griffith as shadow business secretary and act as his deputy.

Badenoch said that as shadow chancellor, Sir Mel had helped the party rebuild economic credibility and become an effective opposition.

A senior Conservative source said: "Kemi is changing the way the Conservative Party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility."

Sir Mel, who was appointed to the role following Badenoch's leadership election in 2024, described his time in post as a "great honour".

New shadow chancellor Griffith said the Tories will deliver "an economic revolution" with lower taxes, Britain drilling again to bring energy costs down, slashing red tape and Labour's Employment Rights Act.

"The Conservatives will always back the risk-takers and wealth creators who deliver growth, investment and jobs," he said.

The Tory source described Griffith as a "no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience".

Opposition parties highlight Andrew Griffith's role in the 2022 Liz Truss mini-Budget

Before he became MP for Arundel and South Downs in 2019, he served as a top executive at Sky and as chairman of Just Eat.

As a Treasury minister, Griffiths defended Liz Truss' 2022 mini-Budget .

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson described Griffith as "a key architect of Liz Truss's disastrous mini-Budget" and said the shadow cabinet featured politicians "who hammered family finances and left our public services crumbling".

That message was echoed by other parties. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "His appointment to shadow chancellor shows they're happy to forfeit any claim to economic credibility in their race to the bottom with Reform UK."

Reform UK shadow chancellor Robert Jenrick said: "They haven't changed and still aren't sorry for the damage they inflicted on our country."

Dame Priti, who had been shadow foreign secretary since 2024, will return to the backbenches and will take on a new international role strengthening the Tories relationship with sister parties and centre-right movements abroad.

Badenoch has selected Damian Hinds as the new shadow health and social care secretary after Stuart Andrew confirmed he will be returning to the backbenches .

Katie Lam has been named as the new housing secretary, after Sir James Cleverly quit the front bench, announcing he wants to run for London mayor .

Claire Coutinho will become shadow business secretary after maternity leave

Badenoch's reshuffle is intended to bring solutions to a number of problems.

First, she wants to retire those members of her top team that have had a relatively low profile, or who have not been delivering sufficient blows to both Labour and Reform UK.

Badenoch paid a warm tribute to Sir Mel but some recent polls suggested that Reform UK were more trusted on the economy than the Conservatives.

And that is something Kemi Badenoch felt needed to change.

Second, while familiar faces like Dame Priti were useful to have in the top team as they brought high-level government experience, they might also remind voters of the party they decisively rejected in 2024.

There has been a changing of the old guard, and Badenoch is now focusing on who can take the Conservatives into the next election - faced as she is by a new Labour leader and cabinet.

Third, she wants to focus on issues where Labour is perceived to be vulnerable.

One such area is defence spending and national security.

So as shadow foreign secretary she appointed Tom Tugendhat - a former security minister and current army reservist who served in Afghanistan and Iraq. He will work as part of a team with the shadow defence secretary.

Some opinion polls rate the economy as the most important issue for voters, above asylum and immigration, and again the Tory leader believes the government is vulnerable here, with sluggish growth.

So she has announced a new Conservative economic unit headed by Griffith, with his extensive business experience.

Coutinho as his deputy is seen as a rising Conservative star who has performed well in her previous role shadowing the former energy secretary Ed Miliband in the Commons, and as a potential future chancellor if the Conservatives were ever to recover electorally.

But the Tory leader has also included the former Conservative chairman and City Minister Richard Fuller in the unit, concentrating on fiscal responsibility and tax.

He will be deployed as an attack dog if - as she believes he will – the chancellor raises taxes in the Budget.

But the role will also underline that the Conservative leader is serious about making her sums add up, in contrast to her characterisation of Reform UK's plans as ill-thought out.

The question now though is whether Badenoch will change her own approach to political leadership.

While some of her top team may be seen as lacklustre, how much opportunity did they get to shine?

She tends to make the big announcements and is ubiquitous on the media.

If the Conservatives are to convince voters they are once again a government in waiting then the public will have to see that there is breadth and depth in the team that is shadowing current ministers.

stories.title: Meta accepts U.S. safety rules while pitching softer tools abroad
stories.summary: As governments consider banning social media for under-16s, Meta is turning to influencers to argue that parental controls are a better solution.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Tech Giants

As governments consider banning social media for under-16s, Meta is turning to influencers to argue that parental controls are a better solution.

In June, Indian actor Hiten Tejwani told his 732,000 followers that “Instagram is okay” in a reel promoting Meta’s Teen Accounts. Ironically, Tejwani had barred his 17-year-old twin son and daughter from using social media until they turned 16.

The reel was made after a Zoom call with Meta representatives, who explained what their campaign endorsed. Teen Accounts, launched in 2024, gives 13- to 16-year-olds private accounts, screen-time limits, and age-appropriate content. Tejwani, who was paid for the campaign but did not disclose the amount, told Rest of World that he agreed to participate because he saw it as an effort to inform parents rather than encourage every child to join social media.

There has been a global rise in the number of such reels in recent months, as Meta pursues influencer campaigns promoting Teen Accounts, particularly in countries that are mulling a social media ban for children under 16, according to a recent report by Tech Transparency Project, a Washington-based research organization.

Meta is using parent influencers to both soften its image and fight back against the existential threat of social media bans for kids under 16, Katie Paul, director of Tech Transparency Project, told Rest of World .

The campaign comes at a time when Meta is facing heat in the U.S. over child safety concerns. On August 26, the company settled a major trial in the U.S., agreeing to make several safety limitations the default option for teens. Australia, Brazil, and Indonesia have already banned social media for kids under 16. At least 22 other countries are reportedly designing and proposing similar policies .

“If countries around the world follow the lead of Australia and enact these bans, Meta will be cut off from young people who are essential to its growth plans,” Paul said.

Meta’s campaign against social media restrictions

Tech Transparency Project found that Meta has been pushing a narrative of safety through “momfluencers” across the world, from India to Canada to Indonesia.

While the campaign plays out slightly differently in each country, the fundamental strategy is this: Meta pays Instagram influencer parents or celebrities with large followings — and in some cases, child safety groups — to promote Teen Accounts, Paul said. A teen account on Facebook or Instagram allows parents to supervise content and communication for under-16s.

“The underlying message is that Meta is capable of self-regulating child safety protection and that bans are unnecessary,” Paul said. “Some of these influencers have hundreds of thousands and even millions of followers, making them a potent tool for Meta’s corporate messaging.”

Meta has also hosted several “screen smart” events across the world, including in the U.S., New Zealand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, to promote teen safety and parental supervision. In Australia, it sponsored a youth mental health service conducting “ safety camps .” In Indonesia, Meta commissioned a survey , which revealed “overwhelming” parental support for teen accounts with safety features.

Influencing controls

Age verification tools are less than ideal, but they’re still better than outright bans, David Green, senior counsel at nonprofit digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation, told Rest of World .

“Mandated age limits are designed to deny young people their fundamental human rights — to access information, arts, and culture, to form communities, to speak, and to play,” Green said. “Age estimation technology threatens all users’ privacy by collecting people’s sensitive, personal information, exposing them to risk of data breaches and government data demands, and chilling speech on sensitive issues.”

Parental tools and youth accounts are a better option than bans, he said. There is probably a role for broader-based social media literacy education as well, “whether that happens through influencers, the government, parents, or peers.”

Snehaalata Shah, an Indian parenting and travel blogger, was approached by an agency for the Teen Accounts campaign. She did not wish to disclose the name of the agency. This was her first paid campaign for Meta.

“They gave us a brief idea where I have to inculcate the teen account features in the middle of the script,” she told Rest of World . “I made a script, and a little bit of changes were done by the agency.” The teen account for her 14-year-old daughter lets Shah keep track of follow and direct message requests and screen time.

“The main takeaway for parents is that there are tools and safeguards available to make social media more age-appropriate for teenagers and to give parents more control and reassurance,” Sonam Jaggi, who runs the account @momavengers with 322,000 followers, told Rest of World . The promo shot by the mom of two kids — 8 and 1 — has amassed 310 million views , and more than half a million likes.

A November 2025 report by a Meta whistleblower and several online kids safety organizations evaluated 47 out of 53 safety features for teens. It found that 64% of the features were broken, missing, or ineffective.

Shah posted a promo reel for Teen Accounts for her 238,000 followers on July 7 — coincidentally the same day Meta published a statement claiming it had “ zero-tolerance ” for child sexual abuse material, and that it had taken down more than 160,000 accounts.

“If every country bans Instagram or Facebook under 16, of course, there would be loss to [Meta],” Shah told Rest of World. She said she recognized there may be a business motive driving these ads. But given that her 6-year-old son knows how to switch accounts on YouTube instead of logging off when the child time restriction notification pops up, she would still promote the tools to protect her teen.

Tejwani, too, is standing by his decision, but as a parent. Although it was a paid campaign to begin with, his heart is in it, and he’s still happy to entertain questions from other parents and media.

“It is compensation we have to charge, definitely. But otherwise, if I’m talking about it right now, if somebody’s asking me otherwise, this is not a paid thing. I will definitely inform everyone,” Tejwani told Rest of World .

stories.body:
The history of technology is rife with copyright panics. In the 1980s, major rightsholders ran to Congress and the courts, claiming that videotape recorders (VTR) were “to the American film producer and the American public as the Boston strangler is to the woman home alone .” Then, the Supreme Court declined to embrace the hype, noting that the VTR was capable of all kinds of non-infringing uses, like time-shifting and cautioning courts to avoid rewriting copyright law in response to new technologies. We believe that courts now should be similarly wary about the hype surrounding AI.

Hollywood’s hyperbole has echoed that of composer John Phillip Sousa , who claimed in 1906 that the player piano and the gramophone would destroy music composition; portrait artists who feared the camera would replace the paintbrush. None of these things happened. Cameras, for example, sparked a resurgence of portraiture and, by making it possible for more people to create image, led to unexpected developments—like the rise of photojournalism.

New markets, new ideas, and new creators are actually what copyright is supposed to promote, not restrict. Using copyright to lock in existing gatekeepers and massive rightsholders’ profits helps neither the public nor individual artists.

Generative AI has sparked the latest wave of anxiety and with it a massive wave of litigation. In multiple cases around the U.S. and the world, rightsholders are asking courts to do precisely what the Supreme Court warned against: dramatically expand copyright protections based in substantial part on hyperbole and speculation. They should decline to do so.

Copyright owners claim that unless courts abandon 300-year-old copyright principles—and give rightsholders the power to control non-infringing works created by others—an imagined flood of AI-generated works will devastate creative markets. Under this “market dilution” theory, building generative AI tools cannot be fair use because those tools might be encourage the proliferation of competing works.

As EFF has explained to the courts in multiple amicus briefs in Concord Music Group, Inc. v. Anthropic PBC and In re Mosaic LLM Litigation , that’s not how copyright works. In fact, accepting this theory would undermine copyright’s constitutional purpose: promoting the creation of expressive works for the public’s benefit. Because copyright law is designed to encourage others to build freely on existing works, it punishes infringement , not competition. The “market dilution” theory would eviscerate not only the fair use doctrine, but also other limits on copyright that work specifically to prevent rightsholders from unfairly suppressing competition by claiming broad ownership over tropes, genres, styles, and so on. In other words, publishers would wield unchecked veto power over any expression that might conceivably compete with a work they own.

The result? Art doesn’t get created, ideas are never expressed, and we’re all worse off. Copyright shouldn’t be a tool to silence future creative competitors—whether or not they use AI in tehir work.

And the plaintiffs in these cases get at least two other things wrong. First, research shows that large generative AI models are unlikely to produce infringing works because the more data on which a model is trained, the less any individual training example matters to any particular output.

Second, AI tools aren’t necessarily displacing human creativity. To take a just a few examples:

Boston-based artist Nettrice Gaskins uses AI to create Afro-futurist art, including a portrait of Octavia Butler displayed at the San Francisco Airport

Indian artists Prateek Arora and Varun Gupta use generative AI to reimagine Western science fiction.

Philadelphia-based artist Alex Smith uses generative AI to reimagine Afrofuturism

with queer, plus-sized Black superheroes.

Ana Miljački, a professor of architecture at MIT, used generative AI to create a “non-liner documentary” film on Yugoslav World War II memorials and the values they embodied.

A research-creation project used AI generated visual art to both amplify the voices of activists in the Iran Woman Life Freedom Movement and evaluate AI’s role in sociopolitical advocacy through art.

AI company Bronze works with musicians like Disclosure and Jai Paul to create songs that never sound the same when played back twice, challenging audience conceptions of what music could be.

It is not the place of courts to say these people are not artists or that AI cannot augment human creativity in a positive way.

Given this range of experimentation, courts should be reluctant to decide in advance what tools do and do not foster “human creativity.” Like the VTR, large language models are general purpose tools, used by humans to do a broad variety of things far beyond generating lyrics. The effects of this particular technological innovation will doubtless be far-reaching, disruptive, and potentially harmful for some—but distorting copyright law is not the way to address those harms.

Watch: Prisoner release scheme "raises more questions than it answers", says shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy

Published 31 August 2026, 08:41 BST

Dangerous criminals could be freed under the government's early release scheme for England and Wales, the Conservatives have warned.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy told the BBC that to prevent one group of dangerous criminals being released early, Andy Burnham was "looking at releasing a different group of dangerous prisoners".

The prime minister said at the weekend anyone convicted of manslaughter would be excluded from the early prisoner release scheme, following a campaign from PC Andrew Harper's family to block the release of two men convicted over his killing in 2019.

He said prison space would be found by releasing some inmates serving indefinite sentences, known as IPPs as well as by deporting foreign prisoners.

Prisoners freed early are returning to jail at rapid rate, governors tell BBC Published 1 day ago

Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost? Published 1 day ago

On Monday Victims Minister Alex Davies-Jones told the BBC: "We will do nothing that would risk the public or put the public at danger."

Under the early release scheme some 4,500 prisoners are now expected to start being released in tranches from October to ease overcrowding in jails.

The numbers due to be released has been reduced after the government said rapists, those found guilty of serious child sex offences and grooming offences and now those found guilty of manslaughter would be excluded from the scheme.

Given that fewer prisoners will now be released than initially expected this will have a knock-on effect on prison capacity.

Timothy said releasing prisoners serving indefinite sentences under imprisonment for public protection sentences posed its own risk.

Between 2005 and 2012 IPPs were given to some offenders in England and Wales where they were considered to pose a significant risk of causing serious harm to the public. Once they had served a minimum term they could only be released once the Parole Board was satisfied they no longer posed a risk to the public. Although IPPs are no longer imposed many people already serving sentences are stlll in prison.

Timothy told the BBC: "By definition, the people who are still in prison on those sentences are dangerous, because they've all been considered by independent expert assessors who have concluded that they are not safe to release and they would be a danger to the public."

He accepted not enough prisons had been built under the previous Conservative government.

Indefinite prison sentences have previously been handed out in several high-profile cases, including to Tracey Connelly, the mother of Baby P, who was jailed in 2009 after admitting causing or allowing the death of her one-year-old son Peter.

There were 2,271 people serving IPPs, according to Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data up to June this year.

Of those, 856 have never been released because the Parole Board thought it was not safe to do so. Ending indefinite sentences for those still serving them would require new legislation, meaning it could be years before space is freed up.

Davies-Jones told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "The government's number one priority is to keep the public safe and in order to do that we need a functioning criminal justice system."

She defended the government's decision to look at indefinite sentences as part of ensuring there were enough prison spaces.

"We need to look at every case on its merits individually, and pass the appropriate legislation and we will do that responsibly and we will take our time to get it right," she added.

She said those released would still be monitored.

Speaking exclusively to BBC Breakfast on Sunday, Burnham said he had applied "common sense" on IPPs.

"I was faced with a situation where people on those sentences who have more than served their time, not being released when others who've committed very serious crimes being released early," he said.

He said the government would table legislation to terminate IPPs by the end of this Parliament.

He conceded that of those offenders, there would be those who would "pose a risk to communities", and a cross-party oversight group would be established.

And there are others who have a more favourable outlook about releasing some prisoners serving IPPs.

Former Conservative justice secretary Sir Robert Buckland told the Today programme that while there are people serving these indefinite sentences who are a "real danger to the public", these are "dwarfed" by instances where people end up back in prison for things like breaching their strict licence conditions.

One such person is Shaun Lloyd, who served eight years following a conviction for street robbery.

Once released, because of his IPP, he remained on indefinite licence. People on these could be recalled for behaviour that, while not criminal, would be in breach of those rules.

His mother, Shirley Debon, told the Today programme that he had never committed a violent crime and called his latest recall "totally unfair".

When Lloyd was called back to prison, he had become drug-free and was near to completing an apprenticeship, she said.

Debon is campaigning more broadly for an inquiry into IPPs, under which she says people are "living in limbo".

Sir Robert said that looking at recall cases like Lloyd's could be a solution for the government.

He added that there was "a very good policy reason" why IPPs were abolished: "It did create uncertainty, not just for the prisoners but actually for the victims".

On the impact overall of changes to the early release scheme for prisons, Davies-Jones told the BBC: "We will have capacity within the system with those numbers but it will be run very tight."

She said plans to deport foreign nationals on sentencing and to re-purpose women's prisons would help tackle overcrowding.

"Our plan is to deport [foreign nationals] on sentencing so that they don't serve a day at his Majesty's and at the taxpayers pleasure."

Asked if these offenders would serve sentences for their crimes once deported, she said "that would be for the determination of their country of origin".

On 3 August, the prison population in England and Wales was 86,495, around 97% of useable capacity.

On Tuesday, Justice Secretary Alex Norris is expected update Parliament with further details on the changes to the early release scheme.

stories.title: Doxxing Safety Part II: Incident Response
stories.summary: Doxxing, also known as the deliberate sharing of personal information to harass or endanger someone, is a tricky thing to protect against. It often happens by some ill-intentioned person accessing publicly available information, then sharing that information more widely in the hopes it will intimidate their target or worse. This guide is a followup from a previous post that describes a methodology for you to clean up your digital footprint and get a firm entry into the art of open source intelligence. There's a slight bit of repetition here, but with a slant towards using those now-familiar tools and methods toward what to do in the context of incident response. The best thing you can do is familiarize yourself with this post and its tactics before something happens, then return back to it for reference when needed. Incident Log An incident log is a way to keep track of suspicious or harmful activity online. It doesn't need to be beautiful or complex, just a place where you can quickly note details around the different things you're seeing online. Noting times, places, people, and the general nature of what you see ought to be enough. In the event that law enforcement gets involved, this sort of record will be helpful. The process of finding and noting hateful incidents online can be incredibly stressful, so now is a good time to revisit the team roles you might have already thought of in the previous blog post . If you haven't yet done that, here's a brief refresher: Assign Team Roles Remember, privacy–and responding to doxxing–is a team sport. Knowing who you trust is as important as identifying threat actors. Having trusted people ready to assist is invaluable in this type of situation. Refer them to this blog post or specific recommendations in it. If you've already plotted out a list of designated team roles, now is the time to remind everyone of their responsibilities. That might look like monitoring the hate forums where activity happens, keeping track of events in the incident log, setting up web alerts, locking down your social media accounts, or contacting law enforcement to reduce the likelihood of SWATing (a type of attack where bad actors call the police on their target, hoping to incite violence or disruption of peace by bringing law enforcement to their door). Through these spliced timelines, it becomes clear that Sophia, compelled by her supernatural gift, possesses little agency. Destiny beckons her forwards. You jostle her through ornate corridors rendered as higgledy-piggledy pirate camps and cobbled Venetian streets. US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles

Having reportedly read Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia.

But Donald Trump’s US trade representative, hitherto one of the president’s less high-profile cabinet members, found himself in that uncomfortable position amid the acrimonious collapse of bilateral trade talks with Canada that now threatens to degenerate into an all-out trade war between the two close trading partners whose economies are tightly intertwined.

An apparent pending deal between Washington and Ottawa aimed at avoiding damaging tit-for-tat tariffs broke down at the last minute, with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, claiming his country had come “under attack” from the US.

Among the multiple and complex points of disagreement was a Canadian accusation that US negotiators had pressed for a weakening of legal protections for the French language, which is most heavily spoken in the province of Quebec.

Canadian provisions include legislation that mandates streaming and online video companies to invest in and promote Canadian content and promote the French language. Carney cast US objections to such regulations as a deal-breaker, and said they amounted to “threats to French language and culture”.

For Greer, a fluent French speaker who once served as a Mormon missionary in Belgium, France and Luxembourg, the charge was too much. “I speak French, too,” he told CNBC , dismissing the claims as “a funny, fake story”.

“My kids speak French,” he said. “One of my kids was born in Paris. So I like the Québécois, and I like that they speak French. What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada.”

The controversy may be the closest glimpse the public will see of Greer being rattled. By Thursday, in what was being being seen by some Canadian officials as a potential olive branch, he was peddling a softer line on the language issue.

“President Trump, myself and the US government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada,” he told CBC , the Canadian broadcaster. “We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important, and we actually champion the use of French.”

The impact was undermined hours later, however, when Trump publicly signed a retributive executive order supposedly changing the name of Lake Ontario – one of the Great Lakes which has shores on both countries – to Lake America. Petty as the act was, it seemed to graphically illustrate the limited freedom of manoeuvre held by anyone representing a president so preoccupied with trade.

And Greer is not the only official seeking to steer the president’s aggressive agenda on trade – raising questions over who is really in control.

Moving the goalposts

Those who have met and worked with Greer describe the 46-year-old – who served as a military lawyer in Iraq, where he is reported to have read Hugo’s classic novel between bombardments – as a model of calm and expertise.

“I have high respect for him. He been pretty creative in terms of trying to thread the needle with other countries as he tries to promote Trump’s trade policies,” said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade representative’s negotiator who has met Greer several times. “From a professional viewpoint, he’s extremely impressive. His reputation as being very level-headed, a very calm demeanor, and not someone who loses his temper or who grandstands.”

It is not known if Greer retained his sang-froid in private as the talks with Canada unravelled, just days after Trump himself publicly declared a deal was at hand.

According to reports, the agreement was derailed after Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, objected to the scale of proposed tariffs reductions on imports of Canadian steel, aluminium and cars, sectors falling under his responsibility after Trump declared them areas of national security under the 1962 Trade Expansion Act .

Carney, explaining why Canada decided to abandon the talks, pointed to disunity among the US negotiators. The White House has denied claims of division between Greer and Lutnick, but seasoned commentators are skeptical.

“Lutnick viewed all this as his turf, and here is Greer, who is the designated guy to be effectively the trade minister, if you think about it in the context of other countries, conducting the negotiations,” said William Reinsch, a senior adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former undersecretary for commerce. “It appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick was.

“From the Canadian point of view, this was a disagreement that developed late in the day and led the Canadians to believe that the United States was moving the goalposts.”

Cutler, who served Republican and Democratic administrations during a 27-year stint as a US trade negotiator, said tensions within negotiating teams were not unprecedented, but were normally ironed out before talks reached the critical stage.

“I think the challenge under this administration is that you have Greer in charge of the trade portfolio, but Lutnick’s in charge of section 232 investigations [restricting foreign import on national security grounds] and that’s where a lot of the sensitive issues are,” said Cutler, now vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

after newsletter promotion

‘Trump whisperer’

Greer cut his trade negotiating teeth as chief of staff to Robert Lighthizer, US trade representative in Trump’s first presidency, who played the leading role in renegotiating Washington’s economic ties with Mexico and Canada, and the former North America Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), which was replaced with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in 2020.

He was chosen for the position when Lighthizer apparently indicated he did not wish to be considered for the post a second time. “Greer plays the same role that Lighthizer played,” said Reinsch, who noted, however, that Greer lacked his former boss’s intimate understanding of Congress.

“He figures out legal ways to do what Trump wants to do, and to get as much of Trump’s objectives accomplished as is possible within the framework that he has to operate in,” added Reinsch. “So that allows him to come back to Trump on occasion and say, ‘there’s a better way to get what you want than what you’ve employed so far.”

Another complicating element may be Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing.

He is reckoned by analysts to be a “Trump whisperer” on Canada, despite a belief that his influence has been marginalized compared with the first Trump presidency, when it was widely joked, according to Reinsch, that Lighthizer was reluctant to travel outside Washington for fear that Navarro would persuade the president to adopt impractical trade policies in his absence.

Navarro, who went to jail for contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with a subpoena from the committee investigating the 6 January 2021 insurrection, vented in an appearance on the C-Span network last week.

Asked to respond to an article in the Guardian by the Canadian writer Jen Gerson, who wrote that US retaliation should be taken as a warning by other western allies, Navarro said: “Madam, your country screws us. You’re in bed with the Chinese and playing games with us.

“Look in the mirror at your tariffs codes. You are the problem.”

Blame game

Navarro has voiced concern that Canada has allowed the import of nearly 50,000 Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles under a most favoured nation agreement, which he fears will ultimately end up crossing the border to be sold in the US.

“Navarro’s worried that the whole USMCA negotiation is really about how do we prevent Canada and Mexico from being a backdoor to Chinese stuff,” Reinsch said. “He would probably have argued last week that the deal wasn’t any good because it wouldn’t shut down Chinese imports in the United States.”

Yet the focus on Trump’s advisers cannot obscure the president’s own fixation with tariffs. Carney referred to agreements being “signed in pencil”, suggesting that Trump would try to change terms even after the details had been hammered out.

stories.body:
Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars

For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country.

Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves.

Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%.

The cratering economy leaves the country’s political class on edge as they try to prevent economic conditions leading to social chaos.

In truth, long before Donald Trump’s latest sanctions push , Iran’s economy had become a parallel battlefield in which the country’s economic commanders were struggling to maintain control.

On 23 August, the US dollar reached roughly 2m rials on Iran’s open market, a new record.

Three days later, Iran’s statistical centre announced that year-on-year inflation in August reached 84.4%; the rolling annual average rate was about 65%.

As purchasing power in Iran collapses, households are buying fewer goods.

Diets are changing, clothes are being patched up and repaired rather than replaced, and medicine is in short supply, though it can be found on the hidden market.

According to the Mehr news agency, demand for red meat fell by 50% in April 2026 compared with the same period last year. There has also been a leap in the consumption of potatoes, leading to shortages.

Basic goods like eggs are now unaffordable to middle- and working-class families, Golshan Fathi, an Iranian feminist, recently said. “They don’t understand that people can no longer afford even a normal life.”

Mohsen Zavaar, a biomedical engineer, said: “For part of the population, the issue is no longer buying a house or a car; the issue is cutting out meat, reducing food quality, postponing medical treatment, and scraping by until the end of the month.”

Frustrated by the inability of officials to tackle the problems, he added: “The people don’t want miracles – they want decisions.”

The crisis has spread beyond food and clothes. Long lines of cars stretched through parts of Tehran and the north-eastern Iranian city of Mashhad on Tuesday and Wednesday as motorists queued for fuel, with some lines blocking entire streets. Many petrol stations, including some of the largest, were closed.

Officials blamed isolated panic buying caused by rumours of a government-planned price increase, or Israeli bombs that destroyed two of Tehran’s three main oil depots.

Inside the government, anxious discussions have been under way for weeks about increasing the price of oil to reduce costly subsidies, but the political class know from past experience that there could be significant pushback. A sudden overnight petrol price rise of 50% in November 2019 sparked week-long violent protests .

Public anger has been exacerbated by an admission that vested interests in the government made it hard to tackle fuel smuggling.

Saqab Esfahani, deputy to Iran’s president, said: “Both political factions in the country are involved in fuel smuggling, and if I were to shut down their operations, they would break my windows.”

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been urged to investigate the remarks.

However, transparency over the economic conditions in Iran is likely to decrease.

Fatemeh Mohajerani, a spokesperson for the Iranian government, said recently that future poverty statistics would only be published with the permission of the country’s supreme national security council, making the decline in living standards akin to a classified state secret.

Iran’s leaders now cast the home front as part of the war against America. Hojatoleslam Taeb, the new head of the Basij paramilitary force and a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, recently delivered a speech that conjured up an image of resistance against market forces distorted by US sanctions.

As part of this war, he said it was necessary to reduce petrol consumption by as much as 10% to reduce the need for expensive imports. Avoiding unnecessary travel would be an act of patriotism, he implied.

But these patriotic appeals increasingly have an air of desperation as the economic crisis becomes worse.

Mohsen Rezaei, the new, more hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, said: “I advise young people to start producing the products they and society need in their homes, just as they gather in public spaces.”

Mohammad Taheri, editor of the economics magazine Tejarat Farda, said the advice reminded him of Mao’s “backyard steel furnaces” during the Great Leap Forward. Mao encouraged people to produce their own steel, with disastrous effect.

Amirhossein Hashemi-Javid, an energy expert, said Iran’s true economic crisis was its inability to export oil due to the US blockade. “The channels for selling Iranian oil are drying up.

“Oil that cannot reach customers from the well provides no revenue for the Iranian economy; it is simply barrels that incur increasing production, storage and risk costs every day,” he said.

At some point, the Iranian government will have to decide if it might achieve more through diplomacy than through continued confrontation.

Only six months on from starting a war, after Trump promised protesters in January that help was on its way , the only commodity the US is now offering Iranians is deeper poverty.

stories.title: How the US-Canada trade war is being felt on both sides of the border
stories.summary: The US-Canada trade war is being felt on both sides of the border.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 31 August 2026, 01:05 BST

The US and Canada appear no closer to resolving their ongoing trade dispute.

Tensions have been simmering between the two neighbours since President Donald Trump returned to the White House just over 18 months ago, and unleashed a wide-ranging global programme of tariffs.

Canada was one of the first countries the Trump administration hit with levies, and is one of two countries to respond with its own reciprocal measures.

Currently, the US has hit Canada's key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles with tariffs, and last week imposed an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods.

Canada has hit back with its own counter-tariffs on American goods, announcing on Tuesday what it calls a "dollar-for-dollar" and "strategic" retaliation designed to match the US tariffs.

With no resolution in sight, how has this enduring trade war affected Canada and the US, and what could come next?

Here are five charts to help break it all down.

Trade war hits Ontario hardest

The tariffs and counter-tariffs have hit some states and provinces harder than others.

In Canada, some provinces have been more exposed to US sectoral tariffs on steel, steel derivatives, aluminium, and autos and vehicle parts that don't comply with the current North American trade deal, known as the USMCA.

Ontario, the most populous province with a significant manufacturing sector, has been hardest hit by the auto and steel tariffs.

Several Ontario auto parts and assembly plants have announced layoffs and production cuts, and the province is estimated to have lost tens of thousands of manufacturing jobs since early 2025.

Metal exports from Quebec - which produces steel, copper and aluminium - fell 36% between February 2025 and 2026, and there was a 3.6% drop in employment in the sector, according to data released in July.

The Royal Bank of Canada estimates that Ontario and Quebec are the most impacted by US sectoral tariffs, while Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island are the least exposed.

Additional US tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods that came into effect on 22 August are expected to impact all provinces in some way, though British Columbia, Quebec and Ontario will feel the brunt.

Swing states in the cross hairs

The US economy is much larger and the impact of Canada's counter-tariffs won't be as stark.

But some states will feel the pain of Canada's retaliation more than others, with tariffs levied on C$28bn worth of US goods from steel to furniture, cosmetics and toilet paper, as of 8 September.

According to data by Statistics Canada, the swing state of Ohio will be hardest hit, with C$3.2bn - or 12% - of its exports soon to be tariffed by Canada, followed by Illinois and Pennsylvania.

For Ohio, it's the tax on steel that will particularly hurt, as well as the tax on laundry machines. In Illinois, where farm equipment giant John Deere is based, it will be the new tariffs on farm and construction equipment.

Derek Holt, an economist with Scotiabank, noted that Canada's counter-tariffs appear to be "very deliberately oriented" towards some swing states that could decide the US balance of power in the upcoming midterm elections.

From the lowest tariff rates to one with the pack

Prime Minister Carney has assured Canadians that, despite the high-profile trade fight, they face some of the lowest US tariff rates compared to other countries.

But with the latest 50% tariffs imposed on a range of Canadian goods, the average effective US tariff rate on Canada is now higher than Mexico's, and is approaching the rate faced by others like the UK and Vietnam.

An average effective tariffs rate reflects the average tariff paid across all imports.

According to data by the Royal Bank of Canada , external , the average effective US tariff rate on Canada in June was 2.9% - the lowest among major US trade partners. It has now nearly doubled to 5.7%.

By comparison, the US effective tariff on the UK is 6.2%. China still faces the highest US tariffs at an average of around 20.5%.

Canada's exports are going elsewhere

Canada, by the happenstance of being neighbours with the world's largest economy, is hugely reliant on US trade.

Their proximity - and free trade agreements in place since the 1980s - has allowed the two countries to develop one of the world's most deeply economically integrated trading relationships.

The US buys more than 70% of Canadian exports, and is a top US trading partner alongside Mexico and China.

But the tariff fight has already started to shift Canadian businesses to other markets. Carney has pledged to double Canada's non-US exports over the next decade.

Bank of Canada statistics suggest that Canadian firms are exporting more to countries other than the US since Trump's return to the White House in January 2025.

Some businesses are adapting to find customers elsewhere.

Matteo Sgaramella, who owns Toronto-based menswear clothing company Outclass, told the BBC he has started attending trunk shows in Paris instead of New York, helping him reach more customers in Europe.

"The reception has been amazing," he said, adding that some European stores are particularly enthused about supporting Canadian products due to the ongoing trade war with the US.

"We're kind of seen as the one country that's kind of standing up to the Americans right now," Sgaramella said.

Other businesses, however, are struggling to diversify their trade, particularly in Ontario manufacturing sectors that are deeply integrated with the US.

A recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pointed out three such regions in Ontario - Oshawa, London and Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo - as being particularly vulnerable.

"These cities remain heavily tied to the US market, while growth in exports outside the US has been limited or insufficient to offset broader weakness in trade activity and local economic conditions," the report said.

While some businesses are lagging, foreign direct investment into Canada hit C$96.8 billion in 2025, the highest inflow of capital to the Canadian economy since 2007.

Canada's economy also strongly rebounded in the second quarter of 2026 to 3.3% growth in the country's GDP, thanks to a jump in exports and domestic investment.

These latest figures have warded off recession concerns, at least for now.

Carney is hoping to attract even more investment. In September, his government will host the first-ever Canada Investment Summit, bringing major investors, CEOs and business leaders to Toronto for two days.

Fewer jobs and less disposable income

On both sides of the border, tariffs have hit jobs and disposable income.

According to an analysis commissioned by Canadian American Business Council (CABC), if the US and Canada allow the USMCA to fail, there would be tens of thousands of jobs lost, primarily in the manufacturing industries directly affected by tariffs and that are highly reliant on the US market.

Around 55,000 manufacturing jobs have already been lost in Canada from January 2025 to January 2026, according to Bank of Canada data.

Not all figures are bad, however, as employment has steadily risen in Canadian sectors that are not vulnerable to US tariffs.

But there is a risk of further Canadian job losses due to the recent 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration.

Calgary-based economist Trevor Tombe estimates that a total of 90,000 jobs across Canada could be lost if these new US tariffs persist.

In the US, the non-partisan Center for American Progress estimates , external that Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, placed last year on dozens of America's trade partners, have also led to tens of thousands of jobs lost manufacturing, transportation and warehousing sectors.

Even for those whose jobs remain secure, the tariffs have meant higher sticker prices on everyday items.

The US-based Tax Foundation estimates , external that an American household could pay $840 more on average this year due to Trump's tariffs on a number of nations, including Canada.

Canada's counter-tariffs are much more targeted and are designed to limit the impact on Canadian consumers, but economists say businesses will likely now pay more to manufacture goods, as a bulk of the taxes will be applied on industrial supplies imported from the US.
