Sir James Cleverly has announced he intends to run for mayor of London

Published 31 August 2026, 09:54 BST

Sir James Cleverly, who resigned from the shadow cabinet on Saturday to run for mayor of London, has accused the prime minister of waging a "war on London" and pursuing a "very anti-London agenda".

The senior Conservative claimed Andy Burnham's devolution drive would come at the expense of London, arguing the plans centralised power in Manchester.

On Saturday, Sir James announced he was quitting the Tory front bench as shadow secretary of state for housing, communities and local government to run for City Hall at the next mayoral election in 2028.

A government spokesperson said devolution plans would "deliver good growth in every postcode".

The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, is halfway through his third term and has neither confirmed nor ruled out standing again.

Speaking to LBC on Sunday, Sir James said Burnham was "stripping hundreds of millions of pounds out of the budget of London councils".

The government's fairer funding review, launched while Sir Keir Starmer was Labour leader, could see some London councils face cuts to their funding settlements as part of a bid to redirect money to more deprived areas.

The government has defended the changes, arguing it is "fixing an outdated funding system" where some of the wealthiest parts of the country "benefited from exceptionally high levels of government support, while communities facing greater pressures lost out".

Sir James, the MP for Braintree in Essex, said Burnham was "blaming London for London's own success".

He added: "The UK cannot be successful as a country unless London is successful as a city. And I see this in Braintree.

"Andy Burnham just doesn't get it.... He's got a war with London, and London needs someone to fight its corner."

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said they were working with local leaders across the country, including in London, to deliver "good growth".

"This isn't about boosting other cities at the expense of the capital – London and all other places with mayors benefit from the set of devolved powers and budgets on offer as we continue to shift power away from Westminster and back to local people," they said.

stories.body:
With traditional goals such as stability and home ownership feeling out of reach, young people are focused on the present

B y now, we all know the shape of financial nihilism: the throw-your-money-at-anything reaction to the dissolution of the slow, linear path to wealth; the prediction markets , meme stocks , cryptocurrencies and microluxuries growing in its place. We’re left in an economic no man’s land. But financial nihilism only describes where we put our money. What about how we earn it in the first place?

The modern economy has long relied on our need for stable employment – to pay the mortgage, to keep our kids fed, or, for some, to chase prestige and power – to generate the work ethic that keeps the wheel of production turning. None of this is going well for young people. Our jobs are insecure , we can’t afford houses, we’re deferring having kids (if we have them at all), and only 6% of us say a leadership position is our primary career goal. Hope is one of the economy’s most productive inputs, powering our willingness to endure long hours. When the production function of income – the mechanism that turns hard work into a stable salary, then a mortgage, then a pension – breaks down, so does our relationship with the input. I call this production nihilism: my generation’s growing indifference to the kinds of work we’re willing to participate in, and where we’re willing to earn.

“Normal people are asleep. Good,” a young woman running her craft business at night-time tells the camera in Shopify’s latest commercial. Partially thanks to all-in-one e-commerce platforms like Shopify, many of us have mastered the art of polyworking. These are jobs our high school career advisers could hardly have imagined – platforms such as Mercor, where white-collar workers train LLMs to do their job; “ YouTube empires ”; the much-covered millions being made by young women on OnlyFans; non-sexualized escorts . Some are supplementary, some are enough to eventually become a primary source of income. Americans seem to be coming around to the idea of “portfolio careers”, with more than half calling them more desirable than traditional careers for a future workforce.

Take away the feasibility of long-term goals and our willingness to wait for “the good life” collapses. So we redirect our motivation to grind and save into channels that pay out sooner – cash, yes, but also autonomy, flexibility or a sense of identity. Fifty-seven per cent of gen Z report having a side hustle, well over double the boomer rate. Day jobs start to function as financial anchors, paying the rent while our side gigs do the identity work. After all, “writer” plays far better on a Hinge profile than “analyst”.

With no solid formula for our futures, more of us are experimenting with what it means to interact with the economy at all. The cultural counterpart to this economic logic is a series of attitude shifts to work, nervously cataloged as trends: the gen Z stare , or faked productivity . I recently wrote about the slow death of the prestige career , where – thanks to AI – companies no longer require a robust team of entry-level workers to scale.

We’re living through a transition in our economic relationship with the future. The cultural theorist Lauren Berlant described how an “anticipatory present” kept people bound to an economic system: enduring the short term in the hope for a promised version of the long term. Profoundly unable to imagine – let alone attain – a prosperous future, young people may be among the first generations to name this for what it is: foreclosed . When the promise of a future stops working, we “maxx” for the present, extracting value as quickly as possible with whatever assets late-stage capitalism permits us to spend. It’s the other side of the “ little treat ” economy.

Neoliberalism, the system that raised us, offers a convenient way forward: everything can be commodified if we try hard enough. When western society was first learning this lesson, France’s artists gave voice to the unease of their postwar consumer boom. The film-maker Jean-Luc Godard’s Two or Three Things I Know About Her follows Juliette, a Paris housewife, as she prostitutes herself to keep up with the lifestyle being aggressively marketed to her. She decides to sell her afternoons, her time, her body. It’s a precursor, in many ways, to the gig economy of platform capitalism: Juliette optimizes any assets at her disposal to enjoy the present moment.

The New Wave tried to warn us against the relentless tide of commodification. But where Godard and his contemporaries channelled their anxiety through women as objects, gen Z reclaims Juliette’s image – not as a helpless, bored object, but as subject. We are agents of our own relationship with the economy. Less despairing, less passive, less accepting: gen Z’s nihilism feels distinctly active. Production nihilism leans into a new definition of work, forcibly detaching us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearly stopped delivering . Nietzsche described nihilism of this kind as a process of clearing away dead values. Which is what production nihilism does: it detaches us from the neoliberal “good life” fantasy that’s clearly stopped delivering . Refusing to accept the current economic system as the endpoint of our search for meaning, we improvise a new set of values as we go.

But is there real agency here? There’s an idea circulating in Silicon Valley: that “high-agency” individuals – those who think for themselves and act without being told – will be the ones to survive the coming AI disruption . This isn’t really agency. It’s the anticipatory bind Berlant warned us about, another story about how to succeed in an economy where fewer of us will realistically be able to. No wonder we’ve stopped caring about where our income comes from, when its source no longer determines where we end up.

Alice Lassman is an economist who writes The Intimacy Economy, a Substack and forthcoming book on the economics of connection, care and relationships

stories.summary: A survey by the party suggested almost half of teachers reported considering quitting the classroom in the next five years.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Lib Dems say schools are approaching an "existential crisis" in teacher retention

Published 31 August 2026, 02:53 BST

Burnt out teachers urgently need better working hours and more support to stop them leaving the profession, the Liberal Democrats say, as the new term approaches.

Nearly half of the teachers surveyed by the party in England said they were planning to quit the classroom in the next five years, with many saying they felt overworked and stressed.

The Lib Dems are urging new Education Secretary Lucy Powell to fully fund teachers' pay, rather than raiding school budgets to cover increases, and to bring in limits on overtime.

The Department for Education said last year saw the lowest rate of teachers leaving the profession since 2010 but acknowledged there was "more to do".

The survey asked more than 900 teachers, headteachers and Special Educational Needs Coordinators (SENCOs) across England how long they planned to stay in teaching.

Almost half of those in post said they were considering leaving teaching in the next five years, while one in ten were planning to spend less than a year in the job.

More than three quarters of those surveyed, which included former teachers, said they had felt "frequently or constantly burnt out" while at work.

Respondents cited high workloads on marking, lesson preparation and other tasks, which they said gave them less time in the classroom.

The Liberal Democrats' schools spokesperson Caroline Voaden said this pointed to a government that is "not listening" to the profession.

"We rely on teachers to educate our children, the least we can do is make sure they want to come back after the summer," she said.

Teacher retention is a challenge successive governments have had to grapple with.

The National Education Union (NEU) reported that 4 in 10 teachers were planning to quit over "huge workloads and excessive accountability" in 2019.

This latest survey was also conducted with the help of the NEU, as well as the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL).

"After over a decade of austerity and chronic underfunding in our schools the system is on its knees" said the NEU's general secretary Daniel Kebede.

"The new academic year is the perfect time for Andy Burnham to signal a fresh start for our schools" he added.

"That means fully funding the pay award and properly funding all our schools and colleges to stem the recruitment and retention crisis and give children the education they deserve."

"As Lucy Powell enters her first term as education secretary the Liberal Democrats are calling for her first act to be to introduce an emergency package of 'back to school' measures to face this crisis head on," Voaden said.

The Lib Dem proposals include the government fully funding teacher's pay, which will increase in England by 3.5% from September, with an additional 3% the year after.

Currently, half of the pay increase will come from existing school budgets.

The party is also calling for proper enforcement of teacher's legally mandated working hours, the introduction of reasonable limits on overtime, and for all schools to be required to introduce flexible working policies.

The party did not identify where funding might come from to pay for the policies.

An education department spokesperson said: "We know teachers do an incredible job and we're determined to make sure that dedication is matched with the right support.

"Last year saw one of the lowest rates of teachers leaving the profession since 2010, and a record number of teachers returning to the classroom, but we know there's more to do.

"We're taking action by announcing pay awards of almost 17% over two years, funding schools to improve maternity pay and offering targeted support to normalise flexible working and manageable workloads so that more teachers stay in our classrooms and thrive."

stories.body:
Nepal requests foreign ⁠help in identification and storing of bodies, DNA testing and rescuing people from tunnels

Visual guide: how the deadly flooding unfolded

New flood fears and a race to free group trapped in tunnel

Poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal on Saturday as the search for thousands of missing people in areas devastated by catastrophic flash floods along the border with China continued.

The combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 691 dead and more than 3,000 people missing after China’s latest update on Sunday. Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, while Nepal’s disaster agency said late Saturday that the death toll had climbed to 675 with 2,498 people missing.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far.

Seven bodies have also been recovered in India from rivers flowing from Nepal and are believed to be flood victims.

The missing list includes 517 foreigners and 933 workers on hydropower projects on the river where the torrent smashed down, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

A number of rescue workers are also missing, including 45 Nepali army soldiers and 40 police officers.

When a Chinese rescue team reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time on Friday, they found “nothing but ruins”.

Surveillance camera footage from the complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only ⁠on Friday were rescuers able to reach the area.

Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign ⁠help in specialised and technical areas, but not in search and rescue. On ⁠Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage ​the rescue ​efforts on its own for ​now and declined foreign involvement.

The areas in which Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing, rescuing people stuck in tunnels, and storing bodies for longer durations, the foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said late on Friday.

Khanal said ​there was no ​need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.

Nepal has requested that its neighbours, India and ​China, provide bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges have been destroyed.

So far, India has sent three flights carrying about 60 tons of relief material to Nepal, including blankets, medicines, food and water purification tablets, ⁠and a specialised tunnel rescue team.

China has also dispatched five tunnel experts from Tibet to Nepal for flood-related rescue work, Chinese state media reported, as the country called for emergency aid to be sent to disaster-hit areas and for international rescue cooperation.

Rescuers – including army personnel and police – have been clawing through mud and using drilling equipment to reach more than 100 people trapped inside a hydropower tunnel in Rasuwa. More than 350 people have already been evacuated from the site under “extremely risky” conditions and the office of Nepal’s prime minister said the rescue effort had become “extremely challenging” due to adverse weather.

Search and rescue operations were temporarily halted because of rain and fog but resumed on Saturday afternoon after the weather improved.

Kawan Koirala, a rescue worker from the Nepal Scout Disaster Response Team, said they had been struggling in thick, leg-sucking mud. “People want their family member’s body back, either dead or alive, but we cannot find them … you can see the mud,” he told Agence France-Presse, exhausted after an 18-hour shift.

Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.

Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.

China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geohazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be ‌unstable and that more than 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.

In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.

China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of ​the highest national priority.

In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events. The BBC and New York Times have reported that videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.

Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.

The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s belt and road network linking the country to south Asia, with logistics zones and vehicle parks built there in the past decade.

Nepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Waglé, estimated the country will ⁠need $4-$5bn (£3-£3.7bn) for rebuilding. “This is just an ​estimate. Loss and ⁠damage is ​being assessed,” he ​said.

More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.

Some of the bodies being recovered had decomposed beyond recognition and will need to be identified using DNA samples, Nepali officials have said.

Nepal government calls for specialised assistance from neighbouring countries to aid rescue efforts

The Nepalese government has requested “specific and specialised assistance” from neighbouring countries to aid search and rescue efforts.

This includes assistance with opening tunnels where people are trapped, technologies that can help locate people alive in affected areas, rapid forensic and DNA analysis, and mortuary facilities for the proper storage of bodies, Nepal’s ministry of foreign affairs said in a statement.

It added: “An 11-member specialised technical reconnaissance team for tunnel rescue from India has been mobilised and a tunnel rescue team from China is expected to arrive very soon.”

Closing summary

We’re wrapping up the Nepal-Tibet flash flood for the time being. Here are the latest developments:

Nearly 3,000 people are missing . Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554. This includes at least 777 foreigners and 933 workers on hydropower projects on the river where the torrent smashed down.

The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 675, the country’s disaster authority has said. China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet– where information is under the strict control of Chinese authorities – that brings the death toll for the disaster to 682.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

Nepal rescuers send air pipe into tunnel with trapped workers. Nepali army rescuers sent air pipes into tunnels, in the hopes of reaching missing hydropower workers, AFP reported . Rescue efforts are focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.

Nepal’s government has appealed for foreign support to aid rescue efforts. This includes financial aid and freezers to preserve bodies. Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, says reconstruction efforts could run into “billions of dollars” , AFP reports. He added: “We will do loss and damage research and then we plan, but I am reaching out to our international community for support.”

Nepali Americans express frustration with US response to floods in Nepal

Lok Darjee and Catherine Guerrero Knight

Amid the devastating catastrophe in Nepal , Nepali Americans are expressing growing frustration with the US government’s response to the crisis in Nepal .

Tsomo Dasel, 40, is the owner of Himalayan Yak, New York’s first Nepali restaurant. Back home in Nepal, her husband’s family is safe – but it’s not just her loved ones that she’s worried about. Dasel said the priority in the aftermath should be to exhaust all available resources to find the missing. Each passing moment is crucial to the search, which she fears won’t match the enormity of the disaster.

She voiced her distaste with the Trump administration’s humanitarian response, after the state department pledged an initial $500,000 in emergency aid for Nepal – an amount she called an “insult” to address a catastrophe with a death toll that’s in the hundreds, and still rising.

“It’s a joke – if you don’t want to do anything, then don’t do it,” Dasel said.

For Nepali and Tibetan communities thousands of miles away in New York and across the US, the catastrophe is has sharpened the focus on an urgent injustice: who is being forced to bear the consequences of a warming planet, and why should communities that contributed so little to the climate crisis bear some of its greatest costs?

The disaster has also arrived at a particularly fraught political moment, as the US has retreated from international climate commitments while dramatically reducing foreign aid and humanitarian assistance , leaving vulnerable countries with fewer resources to prepare for and recover from disasters.

Dasel said that she is ready to help out in any way she can, in a time when “The world needs to pay attention.”

“We don’t know how we can help them … so we’re sitting down together, like, OK, what are the resources? … Maybe their emergency needs … anything that, you know, they may not have, and we can provide them.”

When the time comes, she’ll be ready: “Whatever the team needs.”

We have satellite images showing the extent of destruction before and after the floods in Nepal .

Rescuers successfully gain access to hydropower site, and proceed with next steps - BBC

Biraj Bhakta Shrestha, the Nepalese energy minister , says a hole has successfully been drilled into a tunnel used to carry cables, BBC reports .

Initial inspection has revealed there is no debris inside, he says, but no communication has been established with anyone inside .

He shared that air is being pumped in; if the weather allows, the rescue team will work through the night to make a hole large enough to fit a person.

There is a risk that the rescue operations may be affected by and even suspended due to rain.

We have images of relatives gathered outside of Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital in Maharajgunj, Kathmandu, in search of any information regarding their loved ones who are unaccounted for in the aftermath of the devastating floods in Nepal .

We have new images of volunteers preparing relief supplies for Nepal flood victims coming in.

Here's a recap of what we know so far:

Nearly 3,000 people are missing . Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554. This includes at least 777 foreigners and 933 workers on hydropower projects on the river where the torrent smashed down.

The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 675, the country’s disaster authority has said. China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet– where information is under the strict control of Chinese authorities – that brings the death toll for the disaster to 682.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border has decreased. Satellite images suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border ⁠at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.

People warned against drone use in flood-hit areas, BBC reports. Nepal’s disaster response agency has warned people against flying drones in flood-hit areas, saying unauthorised drones operating in affected areas are “posing serious safety risks” to rescue helicopters and interfering with search operations.

Nepal rescuers send air pipe into tunnel with trapped workers. Nepali army rescuers sent air pipes into tunnels, in the hopes of reaching missing hydropower workers, AFP reported . Rescue efforts are focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.

Nepal’s government has appealed for foreign support to aid rescue efforts. This includes financial aid and freezers to preserve bodies. Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, says reconstruction efforts could run into “billions of dollars” , AFP reports. He added: “We will do loss and damage research and then we plan, but I am reaching out to our international community for support.”

Authorities seek freezers to preserve bodies amid rescue missions – BBC

The Nepali foreign minister, Shisir Khanal , has asked for foreign support to help provide freezers to preserve the bodies of flood victims, as they work to identify and reunite them with their loved ones, BBC reports .

Khanal said as rescue missions continue, authorities are facing the challenge of “very limited” space to preserve bodies.

“There is a risk of fast decomposition because these bodies have been in water for a long time,” he said.

He says he is seeking active support from foreign governments to find ways to help preserve the bodies.

The death toll has surpassed 600 with more than 3,000 people still missing.

Aussie found safe as rescuers search for missing

An Australian woman unaccounted for in the Nepal flooding disaster has been safely located by Australian consular officials.

Cara Severino made contact with Australian officials on Saturday and is safe, Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed in a post shared to social media.

“I spoke directly with her a short time ago and am very pleased to know she is safe,” Wong posted.

“This is a rare piece of positive news amid a disaster that has brought immense loss and uncertainty,” she added.

Wong concluded her post reiterating Australia’s commitment to work closely with local authorities to locate and assist those affected.

People warned against drone use in flood-hit areas – BBC

Nepal’s disaster response agency has warned people against flying drones in flood-hit areas, BBC reports .

The agency says unauthorised drones have been operating in affected areas, “posing serious safety risks” to rescue helicopters and interfering with search operations.

Anyone flying drones without permission will face legal action, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) says.

Daughter traces mother and aunt’s last known location in Nepal through TikTok video

The daughter of a woman missing in Nepal has shared how she traced her mother’s location through a TikTok video posted hours before the devastating flash flood hit.

Tulshi Patel’s mother, Hemangini Jitendra Patel, and her aunt, Hema Sunil Amin, set off on a pilgrimage in which they had planned to travel into Tibet but the pair have not been contactable since the flash floods hit.

Patel, a pharmacist from Milton Keynes, England, said in an interview with LBC’s Matt Frei that she had last spoken to her mother and aunt on Monday, had received a photo of them on Tuesday, and their last known location had come from a GPS signal from the tour group at a place called Friendship Bridge at the Nepal-China border.

“We did our own deep-dive research and we found a TikTok video that verified and showed my mum and auntie and three other people from the tour at the border waiting to cross, I guess, that the local Nepali tour guide had made,” Patel said.

Patel said she had messaged the two women “in the hopes that maybe we’ll see a tick to say they’ve seen it or read it” and had attempted to contact the tour guide: “We’ve messaged the tour guide in case he has a signal because he’ll have a local Sim as well.

“Every day we’re calling via WhatsApp … We’ve not given up, but, from our end, all we can do is research, but we just need kind of eyes and ears there from our side to basically get them out. Get all of them out and safe.”

Nepal rescuers send air pipe into tunnel with trapped workers

Nepali army rescuers sent air pipes into tunnels, in the hopes of reaching missing hydropower workers, AFP reported .

Nepal’s government says more than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside tunnels at hydropower projects, with rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.

Those trapped are among 933 hydropower workers missing since a wall of mud and debris swept down on Wednesday morning, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

“We have already started sending air through the small opening, and we will now begin excavation work and send the rescue team inside,” Sudan Gurung, the Nepali home minister , said in a statement obtained by AFP.

The Ministry of Energy reported that “partial success has been achieved in the drilling operation”, adding that “efforts have begun to try to send a camera and oxygen into the tunnel”.

Rescuers continue to work to clear “the mud accumulated inside the tunnel”, it added.

stories.title: Doxxing Safety Pt I: Prevention and Footprint Management
stories.summary: Doxxing is the deliberate disclosure of personal information in order to bully, harass, intimidate, or instigate a chain of harms against someone. It's a tricky thing to protect against when the jerk doing it is often able to use legal and accessible means to do so. The odds are stacked against everyday internet folk when there's little to no comprehensive data privacy legislation keeping us safe. The responsibility is on each of us to protect ourselves, but the good news is that there's a lot you can do to reduce your digital footprint and take control of your data. This post is part one of a two-part series discussing safety and response to doxxing. This first part focuses on prevention and ways to reduce your overall footprint. The second focuses on incident response, as in, steps to take if you're in the midst of being doxxed. There will be some crossover and redundancy between these two posts, so it's worth reading each and gaining familiarity with the steps well ahead of time. OSINT Open source intelligence (OSINT) is a broad term within information security. It focuses on the tools and means available to us for investigation and information retrieval. OSINT sits at the heart of doxxing campaigns but is also an important part of the process of preventing them. Typically it is a way of describing a methodology of piecing together scraps of information to form a dossier on a subject. There are fancy multipurpose tools (like Maltego or Lampyre) that combine many datapoints into accessible graphs and datasets. As helpful as they can be for traditional penetration tests or corporate OSINT campaigns, they’re best used for investigations focused on organizations, mapping together details like employee email charts, LinkedIn profiles, and company network maps. They may not fit the needs of everyday people or liberation movement workers. Instead, we recommend referring to different OSINT resource lists that index together a bunch of different tools, then using those resources to create a list for yourself of which tools may be most helpful. Many, if not all, of the resources we cover below will be referenced in those guides, and themselves fall under the OSINT category. stories.title: Privacy on the Map (Part 2): Progress, Pitfalls, and the Fight for Enforceable Location Data Protections
stories.summary: Regulating commercial location tracking has reached a turning point. Last year, we published our rubric for what comprehensive and protective location privacy laws should look like, outlining the baseline standards states should meet to shield individuals from pervasive location surveillance. Since then, state lawmakers across the country have begun responding to calls like these, with Connecticut , Maryland , New Jersey , Oregon , and Virginia enacting new consumer privacy restraints on an industry that profits off our physical movements. Yet, even as these states move the ball forward to restrict location tracking, most of their laws leave significant gaps that still must be filled. Other states – and Congress – need to get into the game, too, and ensure protection of everyone. Why Location Privacy Is Important Imagine spending a couple of hours in a coffee shop, a friend's house, or a healthcare clinic, only to discover yourself under police investigation because your cell phone’s location data exposed your presence there. This is the reality of geofence warrants for location data , the controversial surveillance technique recently scrutinized by the U.S. Supreme Court in Chatrie v. United States . Through geofencing, tech companies and law enforcement can map everyone who was present within a specific area over a certain window of time, inverting standard constitutional protections by turning every innocent bystander into a potential suspect. While the Supreme Court's ruling in Chatrie established that accessing location data via geofencing constitutes a Fourth Amendment search requiring constitutional protections, law enforcement demands via these warrants are only part of the problem. That same geolocation tracking is used by commercial data brokers operating in a largely unregulated market . These brokers regularly harvest, aggregate, and sell physical location data to anyone with a credit card (including government agencies, which are among their regular clients ). Especially for individuals seeking reproductive or gender-affirming care , attending a protest , or visiting an immigration law clinic, this pervasive commercial location surveillance represents an immediate threat. stories.summary: This post is adapted from a video recorded by EFF and the Trevor Project. Head over to our TikTok or Instagram to watch! EFF answers all the queer digital rights questions you submit to us through our LGBT Q&A . You asked us: What’s one thing I can do today to improve my safety and security online as an LGBTQ+ person? And for this question, we’ve brought in our friends from the Trevor Project to answer together: Hi, I’m Tommy from the Trevor Project ! The Trevor Project’s mission is to end suicide among lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and questioning (LGBTQ+) young people. Our vision is to create a world where all LGBTQ+ young people see a bright future for themselves. EFF and the Trevor Project know that digital security and online safety can feel overwhelming, especially because we all have different levels of concern for different parts of our online lives. Some might be focused on the dangers of doxxing, another might only want to ensure they're not outed. And queer people can be particularly vulnerable to these kinds of online threats. This might seem like a big task, but the one way you can do today to protect yourself is to revise the information you’ve shared with services and platforms to ensure you’re as in control of your information and data as possible: Protect Your Personal Information Be cautious about sharing sensitive details like your full name, address, school, phone number, and personal photos as it might expose identifying information you want to keep private. Consider using an avatar as your profile picture to avoid sharing your personal photos if that makes you more comfortable. Keep it lowkey when talking about work stuff or sharing details about where you’re studying. Don’t post pictures with obvious spots in the background, like your front door or porch.
